The main reason Adam and I are having so much fun trying to "beat" Treasures of Cathy (i.e. determine whether or not it even CAN be beat) is that we're mapping it, and we both enjoy making maps. Part of the challenge here is that John Collins made the Maze area, which is perhaps half of the overall locale, incredibly difficult to chart, as there are multiple locations with identical names. For example, "You Hear a Wind" is the only location-related text that's displayed in at least three different Maze sites. Being men, we've confronted the challenge instead of running from it, kind of like accepting a dare: "You think we CAN'T, Collins? Watch us!"

During this past Friday night's mapping session at Adam's, it dawned on us that every location's name (or word following "You Hear a..." in each Maze room) is exactly four letters long. This is presumably a requirement of this particular program / array. Also, the vast majority of the Maze locations -- I think we only found one exception -- contain one-way exits in the cardinal directions, but logical, two-way routes in the diagonal directions. All eight don't always apply, of course, as there are plenty of dead ends.

Every Maze location also features a graphical symbol in place of the initial outdoor barn and tree doodles. We originally thought Collins was differentiating his Maze rooms by combining each "name" with a potentially varying symbol, for a sort of Boolean nomenclature (i.e. "You Hear a Howl" plus the empty, white square would be a different location from "You Hear a Howl" plus the black square within a white border); but the wily bastard has displayed the same symbol every time its matching room name appears, even when these represent utterly different locations. The purpose of the graphical symbols therefore escapes me. There's no need for anything except "You Hear a Fart" or whatever. (Well, okay; we haven't seen that one. Not yet, anyway.) Maybe Collins simply felt the need to spruce up every location with more than the text, and these symbols are meant to be the tunnel-shaped views through particular exits, or something equally ornamental and thus inconsequential.

In case this provides any help in figuring out the array, here's all of the information about every "room" that must be stored in a text-adventure program, BASIC or otherwise. I'm recalling these data from my own text-adventure authorship, undertaken a few years back (for better or worse, I hasten to add). Because of memory limitations, no location description, long or short, is seen anywhere in Treasures of John's Wife, so we'll skip that element, as it's obviously optional anyway.

1. Location number

2. Location name
[In this game, it's always four letters long. "You Hear a..." is a constant everywhere in the maze, so "Wind," for instance, is the only actual name]

3. Objects present?
[i.e. things that can be taken and dropped by the player, and could therefore be anywhere -- there has to be a check every time the player moves to a new location. A trick that I always used was to make the player's inventory the highest-numbered location. I knew that I would ultimately have less than 256 "rooms," so it seemed safe to make Room 255 the location of the player's carried objects. That way, if the player were to check his inventory, the program would merely have to see which objects had been "dropped" into Room 255. I have no idea whether or not this method is used in Treasures of Cathy, but it's worth keeping in mind as a possibility]

4. Available exit directions

4a. Are any items necessary for making particular exits valid?
[i.e. will the program bar or kill the player if he tries to exit into a dark location without a lamp? This is always optional, of course, but MAY apply here -- Adam and I have not been able to ascertain exactly what the lamp and rope are for, so we don't know whether or not they've made our mapped exits consistently available]

5. Exits' target location numbers [i.e. "Hey, BASIC interpreter! Room 8, when exited to the east, will bring the player to Room 42"]

That's the bare-bones stuff. Interactions with scenery in more complex adventures, such as Infocom's, are done with simple objects as the scenery bits, large thingies, etc., except that each such object is given the property "Non-Takeable" (or its equivalent variable, of course). This doesn't seem to apply here. Adam and I have not encountered any non-takeable objects that can be manipulated in any fashion.

Chris++

Introducing a new hi-res demo called "The Pixel Stringer". This over 600 byte program is a hi-res addition to BalcheckHR. The intent of this demo is to show piece, with computer generated patterns, many of the tiny pixels in 3 colors on a hi-res screen map. The demo has multiple variations built into the program all to enhance a "modified for hi-res Bally/Astrocade" video graphics experience. Each "show" lasts 16 seconds long. It is very difficult to determine if any "show" is actually a repeat of a previous show.

I started with an idea and after experimenting with the demo during its debugging process, came up with some more ideas to make the demo more entertaining. When watching the finished program, I can't help myself and react with a big "wow!". Adam, you've got to see this demo. I'm hoping a MAME emulation of it can capture what I can see on my 20" Toshiba TV. My hi-res Astrocade outputs a composite video signal using a video driver copied from a Datamax UV-1R electronic schematic, providing a sharp, clean picture.

What is this "Pixel Stringer" demo? Remember the "Critter" program which bounces a critter around the screen. Instead of a critter, this new demo writes just one byte. Pixels 0, 1 and 2 in this byte are set to the background color 00 and the left most pixel 3 is the only viewable pixel. There is no blanking of this byte write. Instead, a string of pixels using the XOR magic function is written beginning somewhere along the x axis or the y axis. The end of the pixel string just keeps growing and growing. When the string bounces off the edge of the screen RAM area, it changes color. The result is a nonstop growing string bouncing around and constantly changing into 3 different colors with multiple pattern variations. In many shows, the speed of the string growth is very fast. I'm talking machine language fast. The following changes are made to every show displaying what seems to be an endless variation in screen patterns:

1. border color around screen RAM
2. first viewable pixel write begins anywhere along the x or y axis
3. delta X low
4. delta Y low
5. write speed
6. new pixel colors (colors 01, 10 and 11)

I had to add some extra hi-res routines, to accomadate the hi-res screen map. These specific routines were not available in my original hi-res test demo, which is also a part of BalcheckHR, so the byte count for this new demo is 600+ bytes. I have about 370 bytes still available for my remaining unwritten short demos. The BalcheckHR 8K byte program package is nearing its completion. I will then test the BalcheckHR board with multiple motherboards I possess and finally write the user's manual doc.

To whomever is able to view this new hi-res demo, enjoy!

Bye.

MCM

15898:
I eliminated the NOP at byte $0000 and put the Astrocade's ROM into hi-res mode and the Astrocade emulator worked fine.

This is the change I made to the first few bytes of the Astrocade's ROM source code:

        DI
        LD      A,$01
        OUT     (CONSM),A
        JP      PWRUP

(Thanks to Michael Matte for suggesting the removal of the NOP at byte $0000.)

Of course, the Astrocade software isn't happy about running in hi-res mode without the proper software, but it does run okay.  I've included screenshots of each program plus the main menu.

Here are some additional details about the game:


Gorf, is a fixed space shooter arcade game with five different screens. Jay Fenton designed and programmed Gorf for DNA (Dave Nutting Associates). It was published by Midway in 1981. Like Wizard of War, The Adventures of Robby Roto! (and others), Gorf uses what has been dubbed the "astrocade chipset".

In 2018, Jamie Fenton (formally Jay Fenton) donated documentation and hardware items to the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, CA. This included Gorf source code and other documentation related to the game. Gorf was not written in machine language, it was written in a Forth-like language called TERSE (Terse Efficient Recursive Stack Engine) that was developed at DNA.

After the TERSE source code for Gorf became available, David Turner, an avid fan of the game, began to use the game's source code to disassemble Gorf and comment it. Details of his work, as well as his in-progress Z80 disassembly for Gorf is in this archive. In Dave's notes, he refers to TERSE and Gorf related documents which are available at the BitSavers archive, here:


http://bitsavers.org/pdf/nuttingAssoc/


In July of 2017, I reviewed the Gorf arcade game:


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21coS6vAjb4


It's great that the recent archiving of the TERSE source code for Gorf is already bearing fruit.

AstroWAV and Ballybin 2 (2005)(Bob Colbert)(beta)[Dec 31 2005]



I renamed the WAV file to cathy.wav.  Then I used Ballybin with the following command line to get the BML file with the BASIC data in it:



ballybin -v2 -d1 cathy.wav



I massaged the data to make it a little more readable using Microsoft Word and ANSI characters which I inserted by holding down the Alt key and then pressing various number combinations on the number pad.  Make sure that numlock is down, or else this won't work.



I replaced the following codes that BallyBin uses:

15908:
The *() array was implemented mainly because the @() array started at the end of the program (+2 addresses). If you added or subtract anything to the program it would change the starting address so what was @(0) would be 2 bytes moved each byte added or removed.The *() array started from the end of the available memory area (NOT the program area) and kept moving toward the end of program. So if there was a SZ of 100, you could put in 49 *() arrays before you would overwrite any data.

Treasures of Cathy - Room and Treasure Listing

By Chris Federico and Adam Trionfo

September 21, 2018, Version 1.0



We modified the game to print the room number (stored in variable A, it seems) by modifying line 30 from this original line:



30 N=0;FOR I=50TO 67;IF *(I)=A CX=13;PRINT " I SEE ",;N=I;GOSUB 5



By adding a PRINT A, like this:



30 N=0;PRINT A;FOR I=50TO 67;IF *(I)=A CX=13;PRINT " I SEE ",;N=I;GOSUB 5



This prints the room number for the player.  Even when rooms have the same names, such as the case of "ROAD" and "WHIR" (among others), the rooms are actually different.



The game says that there are 49 rooms and 18 treasures.  Here is a list of the room and treasures that are in them.  In order to differentiate rooms with exactly the same names, we have added Roman numerals suffixes to the name in brackets.

In looking through the code of "Treasures of Cathy" last night, Chris and I discovered or re-remembered just how different Bally BASIC/"AstroBASIC" is with the flavors of Microsoft BASIC that we're both most familiar with (BASIC 2.0 on the Commodore 64).  Over the next couple of weeks, I may be asking some simple-sounding questions about "AstroBASIC."  This is the first of them.


Treasures of Cathy uses the RUN command in the program six time (on lines 64, 66, 86, 88, 82, and 95).


1) What is the advantage of using RUN in a program?

2) What are the disadvantages of using RUN in a program?

3) Does RUN do anything besides start a program over from the beginning?  For instance, no variables are cleared-out, right?


While looking over "Treasures of Cathy" last night, I stated again just how incredible it is that hundreds of BASIC programs were written for the Astrocade with only 1.8K to play with in most circumstances.


Adam

Treasures of Cathy - AstroBASIC Program Listing

By John Collins

1982



I used BallyBin 2 to get the BASIC code from the digitally archived version of the BASIC game program Treasures of Cathy.  I started with the digitally archived version of Treasures of Cathy called:



Treasures Of Cathy (1982)(John Collins)(2000 baud).wav



I used the following version of BallyBin to get the BASIC data:



AstroWAV and Ballybin 2 (2005)(Bob Colbert)(beta)[Dec 31 2005]



I renamed the WAV file to cathy.wav.  Then I used Ballybin with the following command line to get the BML file with the BASIC data in it:



ballybin -v2 -d1 cathy.wav



I massaged the data to make it a little more readable using Microsoft Word and ANSI characters which I inserted by holding down the Alt key and then pressing various number combinations on the number pad.  Make sure that numlock is down, or else this won't work.



I replaced the following codes that BallyBin uses:



                  Astrocade           Keyboard

BallyBin Symbol   Equivalent          Combination

---------------   ----------          -----------

|INPUT|           INPUT (Words Key)   Alt+0247 - ÷ (Divide Sign)

|*|               × (Multiply)        Alt+0215 - × (Multiplication Sign)

|down_arrow|      ↓ (Down Arrow)      Alt+25   - ↓ (Down Arrow)



There are many more BallyBin-substitution words possible, but I think that "Treasures of Cathy" only uses these three Astrocade-specific symbols.



Here is the BASIC portion of the program.  Note that Treasures of Cathy makes heavy use of the *() array, which isn't included here.



2 NT=0;GOTO 25

26 IF BIF YPRINT "YOU HEAR A ",;E=2×A;FOR Z=0TO Y;GOSUB 6;NEXT Z;↓;GOTO 29

28 PRINT "YOU ARE AT ",

29 I=A-1;GOSUB 5

30 N=0;FOR I=50TO 67;IF *(I)=A CX=13;PRINT " I SEE ",;N=I;GOSUB 5

48 GOTO 9

52 FOR I=75TO 84;C=KP;IF C>48IF C<52IF I=75C=C-48;GOTO 88

86 RUN

90 FOR J=68TO 73;I=*(J);IF IGOSUB 5;IF C=68PRINT " 1=DROP,2=NO";D=KP;IF D=49T=-1;GOSUB 97

I'm going through "Treasures of Cathy" looking at what variables are used.  I've found some suspicious uses of variables that seem like they should not work properly.  Here are two of them:


1) K variable not set in line 6:


6 VA=H;VB=H;FOR I=0TO K;TA=E;TB=F;NEXT I;RETURN


I've search through the "Cathy" code and the K variable is not set anywhere.  I guess that K could have been set when the "AstroBASIC" program loads, but that seems like a poor way to go about things.  But, of course, it's the Astrocade, so it's also an efficient way to save a few bytes.


2) Letter O used, possible instead of 0 (zero) in two lines:


9 CY=-16;CX=O;PRINT "0=COM,MOVE 1=N,2=S,3=E,4=W,5=NE,6=SW,7=NW,8=SE,9=↓


In line 9, CX is set to the letter 0, which is never set in the program (though it might be set on loading).  This happens again on line 20:


20 NEXT I;IF M=0CX=O;PRINT " DEAD END ?";GOTO 9


Being able to go through the code using a word processor is SO much easier than look at the code on the Astrocade's screen or even an old (who-knows-if-it's-accurate) printout from a printer that was hooked up to an Astrocade 35 years ago.


Adam

Treasures of Cathy - AstroBASIC Program Listing

By John Collins

1982



I used BallyBin 2 to get the BASIC code from the digitally archived version of the BASIC game program Treasures of Cathy.  I started with the digitally archived version of Treasures of Cathy called:



Treasures Of Cathy (1982)(John Collins)(2000 baud).wav



I used the following version of BallyBin to get the BASIC data:



AstroWAV and Ballybin 2 (2005)(Bob Colbert)(beta)[Dec 31 2005]



I renamed the WAV file to cathy.wav.  Then I used Ballybin with the following command line to get the BML file with the BASIC data in it:



ballybin -v2 -d1 cathy.wav



I massaged the data to make it a little more readable using Microsoft Word and ANSI characters which I inserted by holding down the Alt key and then pressing various number combinations on the number pad.  Make sure that numlock is down, or else this won't work.



I replaced the following codes that BallyBin uses:



                  Astrocade           Keyboard

BallyBin Symbol   Equivalent          Combination

---------------   ----------          -----------

|INPUT|           INPUT (Words Key)   Alt+0247 - ÷ (Divide Sign)

|*|               × (Multiply)        Alt+0215 - × (Multiplication Sign)

|down_arrow|      ↓ (Down Arrow)      Alt+25   - ↓ (Down Arrow)



There are many more BallyBin-substitution words possible, but I think that "Treasures of Cathy" only uses these three Astrocade-specific symbols.

Yes Adam, everything works great except the up position on all the joysticks and the top row of the keypad.  I don't have a datasheet for the custom I/O chip but I assume the SI0 pin is an input pin which handles the above mentioned controls.  The input pins on the I/O chip have external 8K2 pull down resistors.  Unfortunately, my SI0 pin is now practically shorted to ground which presumably is preventing the affected controls from firing active high.

 

 I verified this again today by removing the custom I/O chip and measuring the resistance out of circuit between the pin 2 (SI0) and pin 1 (ground) which was only about 30 ohms.  The other input pins have much higher resistance.  I also visually inspected the pins and checked the continuity in circuit between the pin 2 (Ken I think you meant #2) and R31.  I'm getting about 400 ohms on both sides of the resistor.

 

 The input pin probably got fried by ESD or I suspect it could have been my audio cassette interface which had some very sketchy wiring.  I don't know how the audio interface works but I know it uses joystick port 3 in addition to the light pen port.
 

 Looks like the custom I/O chip has 2 unused input pins.  I haven't looked, but it might be possible to modify the ROM to redirect SI0 to SI6 or SI7.  Is the source code available for the ROM?
 

 I got pretty good today at playing Checkmate with only 1.5 dimensions of travel.

I stand corrected! I should be 2.

    If you are getting 400 ohms to both sides of the resistor, then there is an open circuit there. one side should read approx. zero ohms resistance, even without the chip in. The prongs inside the socket may be bent and possibly shorting to a grounded circuit. 
    The custom chip is a production mask chip. That means that it is "molded" into a specific circuitry and cannot be re-programmed.

    The only source of the internal connections to it is the actual patent. I have tried reading it to see if I could glean something from it so as to recreate it in another fashion, but all I got was total confusion. I guess that is partly due to the fact that it is PMOS instead of the more modern single power supply NMOS chips.
    The 7MHz and ~7MHz clocks (opposing +10VDC signals) are running through a long series circuit of FETs, alternating between the 2.
I think that made sense at one time. I guess the single +5VDC clock method might have made less sense back then.

Thanks for the useful information about the issue that your Astrocade has with it's I/O problem.  This makes more sense to me now.  Also, Ken gave me a call and explained the hardware a bit more to me, which helped me to wrap my head around the not-quite-dead I/O chip.

Ken mentioned the patent for the Bally's hardware.  If you need detailed information about the way the three custom chips work, then that is certainly the place to look.  90% or more of the information in the patent is completely out of reach for me, but there is some information in there that is useful for someone like me who knows some electronics, but isn't proficient with it.  Here is some more information about the patent:

Bally Arcade Patent - 4301503 (Nov. 17 1981)
"Home Computer and Game Apparatus"
Filed: May 30, 1978.

Abstract:

"A home computer system provides a video processor for use with a television receiver. The video processor can selectively perform a variety of modifications to pixel data under the direction of the CPU of the computer system before the pixel data is stored in random access memory to effectively increase the speed or data handling power of the system."

36 Claims, 167 Drawing Figures.

Here is a direct link to the patent:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/pdf/Bally_Arcade_Patent_-_4301503%20(Nov%2017%201981).pdf

Last month I downloaded pdfs of all of the works cited in the patent.  Well, I downloaded pdfs of all the ones that I could find.  By far, the most interesting one (that I could understand) was the Gun Fight Computer Service Manual.  Since that arcade game is one of the earliest games to use a CPU, Midway actually explains why they ditched pure TTL logic in favor of using a CPU.  It's a neat book to browse:

http://www.tokensonly.com/images/resources/manuals/vol-4-midway-gun-fight-wm.pdf

The beginning of the arcade industry is sewn up, in some ways, inside the unlikely Bally Professional Arcade.  How cool is that?!?

Adam

Yes Adam, everything works great except the up position on all the joysticks and the top row of the keypad.  I don't have a datasheet for the custom I/O chip but I assume the SI0 pin is an input pin which handles the above mentioned controls.  The input pins on the I/O chip have external 8K2 pull down resistors.  Unfortunately, my SI0 pin is now practically shorted to ground which presumably is preventing the affected controls from firing active high.

I verified this again today by removing the custom I/O chip and measuring the resistance out of circuit between the pin 2 (SI0) and pin 1 (ground) which was only about 30 ohms.  The other input pins have much higher resistance.  I also visually inspected the pins and checked the continuity in circuit between the pin 2 (Ken I think you meant #2) and R31.  I'm getting about 400 ohms on both sides of the resistor.

The input pin probably got fried by ESD or I suspect it could have been my audio cassette interface which had some very sketchy wiring.  I don't know how the audio interface works but I know it uses joystick port 3 in addition to the light pen port.

Looks like the custom I/O chip has 2 unused input pins.  I haven't looked, but it might be possible to modify the ROM to redirect SI0 to SI6 or SI7.  Is the source code available for the ROM?

I got pretty good today at playing Checkmate with only 1.5 dimensions of travel.

I took a cursory look at the Nutting source assembly header file: http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/nutting_source_001-015-header.pdf http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/nutting_source_001-015-header.pdf
 I've never done any Z80 assembly, so take what I say with a grain of salt, but it looks like only 1 line of code would need to be changed to redirect the joystick up pin:
 Statement 113 on page 3:  

 CHUP  EQU  0
 to
 CHUP  EQU  6

 

 The above equates the up pin with the corresponding bit on the controllers SW0 - SW3 which are specified in statements 198 - 201 on page 5.
 

 This assumes all games actually use the equates and don't hard code the bit numbers which is probably wishful thinking.
 

 My Astrocade has a single MK36002P ROM chip.  If I wanted to experiment with modifying the ROM, can anyone recommend a readily available pin compatible substitute that can programmed with a TL866.
15925:
There are NO direct replacements because the ROM is masked. There are close EPROMS that would require some pins that need rewiring. There is no WRITE pin, so that one will need to be tied high. There are also a few others that will need changing.They have both CS and OE pins. One of which needs to be tied low and the other needs to go to ~CS pin on the Bally. I think A12 needs to be rewired also.The chip newded is 27C32. The 2732 will work but I would recommend the CMOS version for less current draw.I hope this works.the 28C32 is an EEPROM that can easily be reprogrammed.Please keep us informed on your attempts.

As "rdagger68" discovered, the Bally ROM's source code is on BallyAlley.com in several formats:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#AstrocadeOn-BoardROM

The already-typed version that can be easily changed is the "gold" standard version.  Here is a direct link to that ROM:

www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/BALLY_BIOS_source_code.zip<http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/BALLY_BIOS_source_code.zip>

The "Gold" version of the ROM's source code can assemble to any one of the three existing ROMs by changing one of the following three lines:

BALLY   EQU     1       ; for 3164 BIOS (rare) "(C)1977" and 9999 Gunfighters

WHITE   EQU     0       ; for WHITE body from Montgomery Wards with only 99 men

ASTRO   EQU     0       ; for 3159 BIOS (common) "(C)1978" reverted to 9999 men

Without changing the equate, then the default ROM is the original ROM that shipped with the Bally Professional Arcade units that (possibly?) only shipped from JS&A.  I'd suggest assembling the code to the "Astro" ROM.

The ROM's source code can be changed in an text editor and then assembled from the command line with the ZMac assembler.  I wrote an article called "Programming the Bally Arcade/Astrocade" which explains setting up the the ZMac assembler.  You can read that article here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Programming%20the%20Bally%20Arcade-Astrocade/Programming%20the%20Bally%20Arcade-Astrocade.htm

I really like this VERY unconventional work-around to fix one particular astrocade console that has one bad I/O pin.

This idea reminds me of an article I read by David Small in an Atari magazine in the late 1980s.  The magazine was probably either Antic or Analog.  Anyway, David was comparing the state of the computers in the world.  He had recently gone to Russia, where he was aghast that you could not depend on a CPU working 100% correctly.  Some computers shipped with faulty CPUs that were missing certain instructions in their instruction sets.  He explained that this caused some computers to be unique in the true sense of the word: it was not like any other computer.  Programmers had to taken these possibly broken CPUs into account when they were creating software.  That article was a head-scratcher to me when I read it and it still doesn't ring true-- I mean, come on, how could anyone work with a broken-at-the-CPU- level computer?  You'd have to make work-arounds for everything, right?  Now that "rdagger68" is contemplating doing something on par with what Dave Small encountered in Russia, it really opens my eyes to how fixes can come from very bizarre directions!

Good luck with this quite-crazy, but SO COOL work-around for the Astrocade to get it up and running again.

Adam

Wow, this John Collins fellow, who programmed "Treasures of Cathy" was quite clever.  Well, I already knew that based on his game, but it's fun unraveling this little text-adventure puzzle.

I knew that John had to store the text in the *() array.  I followed the beginning of the program along with my calculator and by inserting PRINT statement at handy places.  For the room names, each element of the array holds two letters in ASCII.  Using some simple equations, John separates each byte of the element of the array into two ASCII characters.  For instance, the first room that I found was the YARD, which is the room where you start in the game.  Here are the elements of the array that I looked at so far:

*(122)=8965  = YA
*(123)=8268  = RD
*(124)=8372  = SH
*(125)=6968  = ED
*(126)=7869  = NE
*(127)=8384  = ST

As you can see, there are three "rooms" here: YARD, SHED and NEST.  Neat!

Finding the names of the rooms, as I figured, would be the easy part.  After I "map out" the room names, then I have to figure out how the directions work to leave and enter from each room work.

It's fun to see what programmers did with just 1.8KB of available RAM.

Adam

My friend Chris wrote me a private email asking some questions about "Treasures of Cathy," but I'm going to answer his questions publically.  Here is what I wrote to Chris yesterday that prompted his questions:

"This 'Treasures of Cathy' information isn't sorted out enough to post to the Bally Alley group, but I did want to share it with my adventuring partner.  These are the rooms and treasures that are stored in the *() array in 'AstroBASIC.'  It looks like most of the missing room are in the house, which I thought we completely explored.  Maye we have to go up or down a chimney like Santa Clause.  Tomorrow I'll try to make in dent in how the directions are figured out in this game.  Check out the rooms and treasures, below [I only include four elements from the *() array here, I sent Chris a complete list]:

*(100)=6669  = "BE" - Room 1 ??
*(101)=6849  = "D1"

*(102)=6665  = "BA" - Room 2 ??
*(103)=8472  = "TH"

Chris replied to me with the following:

"That's pretty damn cool! I'll bet it was an exciting moment when you noticed that the pairs of letters were spelling out the names of locations we'd been to.  What are the first and second numbers in each row? Are they array "slots" followed by lower-level versions of the same numbers?  It's odd that they don't correspond at all to the location numbers on our map (unless I'm missing something)!"

Here is my answer to the questions that Chris asked me:

The first and second number of each row are... hold on, I'll show you an example, then you'll get it:

*(100)=6669  = "BE" - Room 1 ??
*(101)=6849  = "D1"

The first number on the top row is 100. That's the element of the array.  The second number is a 16-bit decimal number that contains two 8-bit ASCII numbers.  The cool thing is that the way that John Collins wrote the program, this can be read simply as plain ASCII.  The number in array element 100 is 6669 decimal.  When the equations in the BASIC program are done breaking-apart this number, your left with two ASCII numbers in the range of A-Z: 66 69.  Here's how the program views this in line 4:

4 GOSUB 3;TV=V;TV=W;RETURN

This line prints these two ASCII letters to the screen.  In a previous program statement, the first number is placed into V.  The second number is placed into W.  The program then prints out the ASCII values of these numbers: BE.  These are the first two letters of the words "BED1"  This is a room, in the house (I presume) that I haven't visited yet.  I haven't followed the program enough to know for sure, but my guess is that the program loops twice through some code to print each room's name.  The first loop prints the first two letters, and then the second loop will print letters 3 and 4 of each room.  Or, that's my theory for now.

Ken sent me some interesting material about the array that I'm going to read over today that I expect will help shed some light on how the program works.

Investigating a game that's very obscure for a nearly-as-obscure home game console is, more than you'd expect, quite a fun project.

Adam

Then add either a line 1 or zero that would load the @( ) array after the main load was done.now write a short program to enter the array data. When done, save that data minus the program to input the array.Now, tell the program once it is loaded to make the first byte in line 0 or 1 a period, which will make it a REM statement each time you rerun without loading it again. 1 way to partially solve that problem, if you have the SZ, is to type in the BASIC program only. Then add either a line 1 or zero that would load the @( ) array after the main load was done.
now write a short program to enter the array data. When done, save that data minus the program to input the array.
Now, tell the program once it is loaded to make the first byte in line 0 or 1 a period, which will make it a REM statement each time you rerun without loading it again. This may sound seem rather confusing, but if you evaluate it you will see that you can alter either part and later it will go together.
Once done, you will need to write a short save line. that will save the program w/data.

You could always convert any @ array to a * array if you:
1) if you already have it in the machine:    you know the total length of the @ array    Have at least 4x the SZ to work with    And write a loop.. FOR x=0TO n;*(x)=@(x);NEXT x    Then edit the entire program changing the @ to * in each instance.
or2) Just start anew and put a * instead of the @ and type in the strings into the *( ) array    of course it will only work in AstroBASIC after that

    You could always convert any @ array to a * array if you:
1) if you already have it in the machine:    you know the total length of the @ array    Have at least 4x the SZ to work with    And write a loop.. FOR x=0TO n;*(x)=@(x);NEXT x    Then edit the entire program changing the @ to * in each instance.
or2) Just start anew and put a * instead of the @ and type in the strings into the *( ) array    of course it will only work in AstroBASIC after that

The directions of movement that can be made from a room in "Treasures of Cathy" are contained in the *() array in elements 0-49 (I'm not sure if zero is actually used).  The room number corresponds to the element number.  See lines program lines 12-24 for some of the BASIC statements that figure-out the possible directions of movement:


12 G=ABS(*(A));M=0;FOR I=1TO 5;IF G=0I=5;GOTO 20

14 G=G÷10;IF RM=L M=I;I=5

20 NEXT I;IF M=0CX=O;PRINT " DEAD END ?";GOTO 9

22 M=M-2;IF M<1M=M-1

24 A=A+M;P=P-1

A=Current Room Number
P=Score
L=Direction Player picked from list of nine directions
G=Value in *() element (this value gets modified)
M=Somehow this will end up helping to figure-out which room to link to next
I=For/Next Counter Value

I'm going to go out in a little while, so I won't have time to work on this anymore until, hopefully, sometime (if possible) tomorrow.  Here's what I figured out so far:

The directions of movement from a room are:

1=N,2=S,3=E,4=W,5=NE,6=SW,7=NW,8=SE,9=Down

Here are five examples (notice that the numbers of each element always seem to correspond to the direction the player can move).  There is some math going on here that I haven't followed yet.

Room 11 - LIV. - Exits - N(1), E(3)
*(011)=13

Room 12 - YARD - Exits - N(1), SW(6)
*(012)=601

Room 13 - SHED - Exits - NE(5), E(3), S(2)
*(013)=23050

Room 14 - NEST (with Key) - Exits - Down (9) [only down)
*(014)=900

Room 15 - TREE (I) - Exits - W(4), SW(6), S(2)
*(015)=2604

Do you see what I mean?  All the exit direction numbers are in each of the elements of the *() array.  Pretty neat.  This is really only a hint of how the program works, but it's a start.  I need to follow this program through some more and start to dig in.  Understanding it is equally as fun as playing it.

Adam

This was a good hint, Ken.  It changed my thinking to find new "pathways" to consider as I hand-traced my way through the "Treasure of Cathy's" BASIC program.



I figured-out how the directions from each room are decoded by the program.  From what I can tell so far, each room can have up to five exits.  A decimal number, from 1-5 digits, is used to determine the next room number based on the direction that the player chooses from the 9 directions, which are:



   NW-7  N-1  NE-5         D-9 [Down]

      \   |   /

       \  |  /

        \ | /

 W-4 ---- X ----- E-3

        / | \

       /  |  \

      /   |   \

   SW-6  S-2  SE-8





I haven't found any examples in the *() array that are only one digit.



The position of each number is used to determine to which room the player will move next.  Let me explain how this works using the room in which the player begins the game.



The game starts in room 12, the YARD.  This is *() array element 12.  The contents are:



*(012)=601



From the above information, you can tell that there are two exits.  Any non-zero number is an exit.  However, it's possible to enter commands such as UP or IN, which are a tenth and 11th direction.  I have not yet determined how these commands work yet.  I'm trying to figure-out one thing at a time.



We know from the value 601 in the *(12) array (Room 12) that that the player can move north and south-west (number 6 and 1 are present).  The position of the number determines to which room number the player will move next.  Here's how that works:



Current_Room_Number (CRN) + Direction_Position_Value (DPV) = New_Room_Number (NRM)



As your eyes glaze over and you wonder what that means, first remember that I'm working backward from the BASIC program.  This seems to work and I've made up all of these names.  Here's a detailed explanation:



The value of the five-digit position is counted with a loop where the variable I counts the current position.  Since I starts at 5, we'll name the positions like this:



DPV5 DPV4 DPV3 DPV2 DPV1



In our case, with room 12, the value 601 works out to be the following:



6 = DPV3

0 = DPV2

1 = DPV1



The values of DPV are worked out using various loops and equations in the BASIC program, but this is what you get each time:



DPV5 =  3

DPV4 =  2

DPV3 =  1

DPV2 = -1

DPV1 = -2



Let's determine to which rooms we can travel based on Room 12's Current Room Number value of 601:



Moving North (1) in DPV1 means we're using this equation:



Current_Room_Number (CRN) + Direction_Position_Value (DPV) = New_Room_Number (NRM)



12 + -2 = New_Room_Number (NRM)



10 = New_Room_Number (NRM)



In this case if we head north, then we end up in Room 10, which is the room labeled DOOR.  When I consult the map that Chris and I made then I see that's right.  If we move south-west then we get:



Current_Room_Number (CRN) + Direction_Position_Value (DPV) = New_Room_Number (NRM)



12 + 1 = New_Room_Number (NRM)



13 = New_Room_Number (NRM)



Yes, that works out too.  Room 13 is the SHED.



I've tried this for several rooms and this equation seems to work each time.  The part that I find confusing, if you don't count tracing-out the code using too much paper and hand-scribbled notes, is how the map was created in the first place.  There must be some equation that allowed the programmer to create the map with the Room numbers on it.  I originally thought that John Collins had a free hand when he created his map, but now that I'm looking at how the program works, at least this part of it, I think he may have been forced to make some concessions with where some of the rooms lead and from.  This probably heavily affects, in particular, the layout of the maze.



Hey, Mr. Chris++, when are we gonna finish playing this game?!? ;-)



Adam

12 G=ABS(*(A));M=0;FOR I=1TO 5;IF G=0I=5;GOTO 20
14 G=G÷10;IF RM=L M=I;I=5
20 NEXT I;IF M=0CX=O;PRINT " DEAD END ?";GOTO 9
22 M=M-2;IF M<1M=M-1
24 A=A+M;P=P-1

A=Current Room Number
P=Score
L=Direction Player picked from list of nine directions
G=Value in *() element (this value gets modified)
M=Somehow this will end up helping to figure-out which room to link to next
I=For/Next Counter Value

I'm going to go out in a little while, so I won't have time to work on this anymore until, hopefully, sometime (if possible) tomorrow.  Here's what I figured out so far:

The directions of movement from a room are:

1=N,2=S,3=E,4=W,5=NE,6=SW,7=NW,8=SE,9=Down

Here are five examples (notice that the numbers of each element always seem to correspond to the direction the player can move).  There is some math going on here that I haven't followed yet.

Room 11 - LIV. - Exits - N(1), E(3)
*(011)=13

Room 12 - YARD - Exits - N(1), SW(6)
*(012)=601

Room 13 - SHED - Exits - NE(5), E(3), S(2)
*(013)=23050

Room 14 - NEST (with Key) - Exits - Down (9) [only down)
*(014)=900

Room 15 - TREE (I) - Exits - W(4), SW(6), S(2)
*(015)=2604

Do you see what I mean?  All the exit direction numbers are in each of the elements of the *() array.  Pretty neat.  This is really only a hint of how the program works, but it's a start. 60 M=(X×X+Y×Y);M=M÷D;M=M÷2

This is based on the assumption that D÷2 isn't supposed to be calculated separately, but rather sequentially, as it's not in parentheses.

into this:

60 M=(X×X+Y×Y);M=M÷D;M=M÷2

I added "Mod 2" by Dan Sandin from "Computer Graphics and Art, 1980-1981 Yearbook 5."

This program can be download here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#Mod2AB


More details about the program follow below.

Adam


"MOD 2," a Bally BASIC video art program, that appeared in an article called "Pix-Art" by Frank Dietrich and Zsuzsanna Molnar.  This article, which appeared in "Computer Graphics and Art," 1980-1981 Yearbook 5, covers the Bally Arcade as a low-cost solution to create graphics using Bally BASIC and the ZGrass language.  It specifically talks about several pieces of art that were written using the two languages.  Some of the video art pictures are included in the article, as well as some source code for a few programs.

"MOD 2" was retyped from a version of the article from the Bob Fabris collection.  The article in that collection isn't a photocopy of the "Computer Graphics and Art" article.  Given Bob's ties to the Bally Arcade community through his Arcadian newsletter, perhaps this is the version of the article that was submitted to the magazine and eventually printed.

A similar article to "Pix-Art" was published in "Creative Computing" (June 1981) as "Pictures by Funny Numbers."  Credit in the article is given to "Frank Dietrich and Zsuzsa Molnar."  I'm not sure which are the correct spellings of the names.

The "MOD 2" program, while written in Bally BASIC, was not given line numbers.  On September 27, 2018, this program was typed into "AstroBASIC" by Adam Trionfo.  The program was digitally archived used BallyBin and AstroWAV 1.4.

Here are the program and its accompanying notes, as they appeared in the "Pix-Art" article:

------------------------------

Dan Sandin needs about 15 minutes to finish a single one of these MOD images, consisting of circles which seem to be mapped onto globes.

     MOD 2

     CLEAR
     D=5
     FOR Y=43 to -44 STEP -1 D=D+2
          FOR X= -80 to 79
               M= (X*X+Y*Y) /D /2
               IF RM = 0 BOX X,Y,1,1,1
          NEXT X
     NEXT Y
     STOP

Some of the important aspects of this compact 10 line program are:

1. Only two nested loops create the basic structure which scans the whole screen.

2. The computation of X and Y squared for each pixel and the RM command which returns the remainder of a division, makes it possible to generate circles even in an integer basic.

3. The size of the circles depends on the value of the division factor-- D.  Their growth is controlled by incrementing D after one vertical line is scanned, thus also generating the 3-D effect.  Without incrementing D the result would be a regular pattern of circles of the same size.

------------------------------

This is the program as it was typed into "AstroBASIC:"

5 .MOD 2
10 CLEAR
20 D=5
30 FOR Y=43TO -44STEP -1
40 D=D+1
50 FOR X=-80TO 79
60 M=(X×X+Y×Y)÷D÷2
70 IF RM=0BOX X,Y,1,1,1
80 NEXT X
90 NEXT Y
100 STOP

"MOD 2," a Bally BASIC video art program, that appeared in an article called "Pix-Art" by Frank Dietrich and Zsuzsanna Molnar.  This article, which appeared in "Computer Graphics and Art," 1980-1981 Yearbook 5, covers the Bally Arcade as a low-cost solution to create graphics using Bally BASIC and the ZGrass language.  It specifically talks about several pieces of art that were written using the two languages.  Some of the video art pictures are included in the article, as well as some source code for a few programs.

"MOD 2" was retyped from a version of the article from the Bob Fabris collection.  The article in that collection isn't a photocopy of the "Computer Graphics and Art" article.  Given Bob's ties to the Bally Arcade community through his Arcadian newsletter, perhaps this is the version of the article that was submitted to the magazine and eventually printed.

A similar article to "Pix-Art" was published in "Creative Computing" (June 1981) as "Pictures by Funny Numbers."  Credit in the article is given to "Frank Dietrich and Zsuzsa Molnar."  I'm not sure which are the correct spellings of the names.

The "MOD 2" program, while written in Bally BASIC, was not given line numbers.  On September 27, 2018, this program was typed into "AstroBASIC" by Adam Trionfo.  The program was digitally archived used BallyBin and AstroWAV 1.4.

Here are the program and its accompanying notes, as they appeared in the "Pix-Art" article:

------------------------------

Dan Sandin needs about 15 minutes to finish a single one of these MOD images, consisting of circles which seem to be mapped onto globes.

     MOD 2

     CLEAR
     D=5
     FOR Y=43 to -44 STEP -1 D=D+2
          FOR X= -80 to 79
               M= (X*X+Y*Y) /D /2
               IF RM = 0 BOX X,Y,1,1,1
          NEXT X
     NEXT Y
     STOP

Some of the important aspects of this compact 10 line program are:

1. Only two nested loops create the basic structure which scans the whole screen.

2. The computation of X and Y squared for each pixel and the RM command which returns the remainder of a division, makes it possible to generate circles even in an integer basic.

3. The size of the circles depends on the value of the division factor-- D.  Their growth is controlled by incrementing D after one vertical line is scanned, thus also generating the 3-D effect.  Without incrementing D the result would be a regular pattern of circles of the same size.

------------------------------

This is the program as it was typed into "AstroBASIC:"

5 .MOD 2
10 CLEAR
20 D=5
30 FOR Y=43TO -44STEP -1
40 D=D+1
50 FOR X=-80TO 79
60 M=(X×X+Y×Y)÷D÷2
70 IF RM=0BOX X,Y,1,1,1
80 NEXT X
90 NEXT Y
100 STOP

I have uploaded J-3 3K Art by Stanley Kendall to YouTube. This is a video art program written for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade in Blue Ram BASIC.It requires at least a 4K Blue Ram expansion. According to comments in the program, it was written on May 28, 1984.


MOD 2, a Bally BASIC video art program, that appeared in an article called Pix-Art by Frank Dietrich and Zsuzsanna Molnar.  This article, which appeared in Computer Graphics and Art, 1980-1981 Yearbook 5, covers the Bally Arcade as a low-cost solution to create graphics using Bally BASIC and the ZGrass language.  It specifically talks about several pieces of art that were written using the two languages.  Some of the video art pictures are included in the article, as well as some source code for a few programs.

0:00 - MOD 2 Titles
0:08 - Overview of MOD 2
12:55 - MOD 2, Program Loads
13:18 - MOD 2 Running, Picture Drawing Begins
15:40 - MOD 2 Running, Picture 1/4 Finished
18:25 - MOD 2 Running, Picture 1/2 Finished
21:10 - MOD 2 Running, Picture 3/4 Finished
23:56 - MOD 2 Running, Picture Drawing Complete
24:10 - MOD 2 Bally BASIC Listing
24:24 - End Credits

Here are the program and its accompanying notes, as they appeared in the Pix-Art article:

Dan Sandin's program needs about 15 minutes to finish a single one of these MOD images, consisting of circles which seem to be mapped onto globes.

Some of the important aspects of this compact 10 line program are:

1. Only two nested loops create the basic structure which scans the whole screen.

2. The computation of X and Y squared for each pixel and the RM command which returns the remainder of a division, makes it possible to generate circles even in an integer basic.

3. The size of the circles depends on the value of the division factor-- D.  Their growth is controlled by incrementing D after one vertical line is scanned, thus also generating the 3-D effect.  Without incrementing D the result would be a regular pattern of circles of the same size.

If you'd like to read the article Pix-Art by Frank Dietrich and Zsuzsanna Molnar, I then it's available on BallyAlley.com.  This version of the article is from the Bob Fabris collection. It's not a photocopy of the Computer Graphics and Art article. Given that Bob was the editor of the Arcadian newsletter and had ties to the Bally Arcade community, perhaps this version was what was submitted to the magazine that eventually printed it.  Pic-Art is certainly worth a read if you're interested video art:

If you're planning on redesigning the Bally / Astrocade PCB I have a zillion suggestions. I have been laying out PCBs since the 90's and there are way too many errors in the Bally design.
To start off with, I would make it a 4 layer board with the power and being the inner planes, using thermal reliefs.move the DATA chip out from under the keypad.
Move the 10,000uF C6 and C1, the 1500uF, lytics to some point nearer to the regulators.U6, U12 - U14 can all be one GAL16V8 chip. The Z-80 can be a PLCC chip and should be a faster "C" type to lower current.The DRAMS can be 4164 chip to eliminate the 12/15. power supply, further lowering the strain on the power supply.Traces can be made thinner so chips can be located closer.The z80 should be closer to the 50 pin card edge connection.With some slight redesigning of the existing circuitry, The memory could be one 64K (or 128K for more common supplying) SRAM chip, or the 8 drams mentioned above.The keypad connections could be either any of the more common connectors to the PCB, Like 0.050", 0.100" or 0.156".You could also look into something metric.
That's just a start.Ken

This 27-minute video uses both versions of Spiral as a springboard to show how video art on the Astrocade began on this system.

Spiral 1 and Spiral 2 are two video art programs by Dick Ainsworth, co-writer of the Bally BASIC instruction manual.  These programs are written for the Bally Arcade game system, more commonly called by its 1981 re-release name of Astrocade.  Both programs are included in the 1978 original Bally BASIC manual and its 1981 "AstroBASIC" re-release.  The video art is created using a few program loops and LINE command statements to fill the screen with a random, semi-controlled, pattern.

Here is a screenshot from Spiral 1:

[cid:ace7c634-703d-44be-b737-79589a1e7f8b]

Spiral 1 appears in the appendix of programs at the back of both BASIC manuals (page 103 of the Bally BASIC manual and on page 75 of the "AstroBASIC" manual).  Spiral 2 is built-up from smaller BASIC pieces in Chapter 8: Video Art (pages 93-96 of the Bally BASIC manual pages 62-64 of the "AstroBASIC" manual).  The chapter explains how the program works.

The eight-page Video Art chapter in the Bally BASIC manual gives users new to programming a chance to try their newly acquired skills to create art.  Spiral 1 and Spiral 2, simple programs that could be easily modified, inspired many Bally Arcade users.  Judging from the printed content of the two main Astrocade newsletters (Arcadian and Cursor/BASIC Express), video games and video art became the two most popular ways that amateur programmers on the Astrocade platforms used their systems.  Perhaps without the video art chapter and these two simple BASIC example programs, there would not have been as much video art created on the Bally system.  That would have been a shame, as the art that clever programmers created on the Astrocade platform over the next seven to eight years is quite impressive given the limited 1.8KB of RAM and 160x88 resolution of the console.

Enjoy this look at Spiral and the general look into video art on the Astrocade.

Electric Doily, written by Dick Ainsworth, is a video art program released by Bally Manufacturing Corp. in 1978 on the 300-BAUD Bally BASIC Sampler that was included with the 300-baud tape interface.  The tape's official title is "Software No. 1 (APC-7001)."  This is the only Bally BASIC tape released by Bally.

Here is a screenshot of the program:

[cid:69621c7a-0388-41bd-9965-bd07d5ca2b1d]



Electric Doily places a random square on the screen and reflects it eight times to create a symmetrical pattern.  Start the program by selecting program one from the menu.  When the program begins, a continuous pattern is generated with music notes.  Pressing zero returns to menu.

The version on the tape runs from a menu of five different programs and it has changing colors and sound.  The printed version, on page 118 of the Bally BASIC manual, is B&W-only and doesn't have any sound effects.  Only the color version of the video art is shown in this video.

Just as a quick fix until someone who knows more about this particular version of BASIC chimes in, why not try breaking up the operation, effectively removing any hierarchal problems:

Change

60 M=(X×X+Y×Y)÷D÷2

into this:

60 M=(X×X+Y×Y);M=M÷D;M=M÷2

This is based on the assumption that D÷2 isn't supposed to be calculated separately, but rather sequentially, as it's not in parentheses.

It's not the most efficient solution space-wise, but I'm guessing that the program isn't right up against the limit. If you still get an error, try breaking up the assignments into three separate line numbers. Then you'll know exactly which part caused the error. (I'm just presuming that AstroBASIC displays which line caused the error.)

15996:
The Astrocade and Ralph Baer

One of the two Bally Arcade/Astrocade patents (U.S. Patent 4,296,930, "TV Game Apparatus") references 31 patents.  Among them are two by Ralph Baer, usually referred to as the father of home video games.  These both refer to patents related to, I think, the original 1972 Odyssey home video game system.  Here is some information about them:

Preprogrammed Television Gaming System
3921161 November 1975 Baer
Abstract
Apparatus for playing games on the cathode ray tube screen of a television receiver is disclosed comprising a gaming device having components for providing location controllable spots on the screen, a source of prerecorded modulated audio frequency control signals, and means for demodulating those control signals and for supplying them to selected gaming device components to thereby provide gaming capabilities where the progress of a game is in part controlled by the recorded signals and in part controlled by the actions of a player. The signal source may be a magnetic tape or record/disc player and a selected prerecorded game tape or disc with control signals recorded thereon as a plurality of modulated audio frequency signals to thereby allow signal separation based on frequency and waveform control techniques and subsequent demodulation of each so separated carrier to provide a plurality of control signals.

Here is a link to the above patent (check out the cool drawings of the console!):


https://patents.google.com/patent/US3921161


Digital video modulation and demodulation system
3993861 November 1976 Baer
Abstract
In a television system, a digital video system permits the transmission of data along with the usual television picture. The television picture field includes one or more selectively addressable areas and the data is impressed on these areas as digital, binary-coded brightness modulations at rates greater than the vertical field rate. At the receiving end of the system, the viewer positions one or more light sensors opposite these screen areas. The light sensors respond to the binary-coded brightness modulations by developing corresponding binary-coded digital electrical signals. The data stream from a light sensor can then be decoded by a demodulator/decoder operated by the viewer.

Here are links for the second patent:


https://patents.google.com/patent/US3993861


It's pretty neat readying/browsing the patents references in the Astrocade patents.  Here are links to both of them:


TV Game Apparatus

Bally Arcade Patent 4,296,930 (Oct. 27, 1981)

Filed: July 05, 1977.


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/Bally%20Arcade%20Patent%204296930/Bally_Arcade_Patent_-_(4296930)_(Oct_27_1981).pdf



Home Computer and Game Apparatus

Bally Arcade Patent - 4301503 (Nov. 17 1981)

Filed: May 30, 1978.


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/pdf/Bally_Arcade_Patent_-_4301503%20(Nov%2017%201981).pdf


Some of the references patents go way back to 1958.  Also, some of them are patents for Atari systems.

Neat!

15997:
I added Gun Fight Computer Service Manual: For the Midway 8080 Microprocessor Game Series, A Comprehensive Analysis of the Gun Fight Game Computer by Midway Manufacturing Co, published in 1976 in William Arkush Video Game Data Books, Vol. 4.  This book is quite hard to find-- it's not the normal version that you find around the Internet in all the familiar arcade hardware websites.


This Gun Fight manual is referenced in the Bally Arcade/Astrocade patent (U.S. Patent 4,296,930, "TV Game Apparatus"). Tony Miller, a hardware engineer who helped create the Bally Professional Arcade, once said that the custom chips in the Astrocade were created from the hardware in such games as Gun Fight. Gun Fight is normally considered the first arcade video game that used a microprocessor (it uses the 8080 CPU).

You can download this 30MB pdf here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/Arcade_Games/Arcade_Games.html#GunFightComputerServiceManualMidway8080Microprocessor


Here is some information from the manual's introduction. Notice how the author's feel the need to explain why they choose to move away from the discrete TTL logic used in former arcade games, such as Western Gun.

1.1.1 Why Use A Microprocessor?

The integrated microprocessor (often abbreviated simply as uP) has caused a revolution in the electronics industry for the contemporary uP now makes possible real computers for only a few hundred dollars. Ever since the advent of video games, designers have often wanted to use an actual, general-purpose type computer to operate their games and, in fact, a few custom games have been constructed using fairly powerful minicomputers. But it has never been possible to use such a computer for production video games simply because the cheapest available minicomputers cost thousands, rather than hundreds, of dollars. But today, with microprocessor chips available for $20 and under, systems comparable in power to commercial minis can be built for maybe a tenth of the cost. Obviously the uP is a reality today and is rapidly changing the face of the electronics industry. But what of the reasons designers are so interested in applying them to video games? After all, video games have been successfully manufactured for a number of years using the random-logic type of architecture, so why change now? [...]

Now that we have discussed some of the reasons that microprocessors are so quickly gaining in popularity for video games (and a tremendous number of other systems as well), it is time to turn our attention to the specifics of the Gunfight game system. In the following pages, we will discuss the general architecture of the Midway 8080 CPU mother board and the Gunfight game board as well as the specific operation of all phases and components of the system itself. In conclusion, we will present a number of troubleshooting approaches for dealing with specific problems and problematic areas as well as providing a generous amount of actual troubleshooting data so that video game technicians with ordinary troubleshooting equipment will be able to fully explore the circuitry found in this game.

This document is originally from the website TokensOnly.com:

"Back when home television games were just a gleam in Ralph Baer’s eye, and the penny arcades were full of B&W machines like Pong, Tank, and Death Race; William Arkush was distributing technical manuals that provided sophisticated troubleshooting information. Since the industry was just getting started, such quality information was very useful when trying to keep location games running. The manuals covered a wide range of subjects for specific game titles, and covered them thoroughly. William Arkush Video Game Data Books - Back when home television games were just a gleam in Ralph Baer's eye, and the penny arcades were full of B&W machines like Pong, Tank, and Death Race; William Arkush was distributing technical manuals that provided sophisticated troubleshooting information. Since the industry was just getting started, such quality information was very useful when trying to keep location games running. The manuals covered a wide range of subjects for specific game titles, and covered them thoroughly."


http://www.tokensonly.com/william-arkush-video-game-data-books/


This book is pretty cool.  If you're into hardware, then this book is written for you!  It's also neat to browse for those interested in computer/arcade history, as the document goes out of its way to answer why the heck would anyone want to put a microprocessor in a video game.  Well, why indeed?!?

Adam
